title: Indra's net
hook: a net of jewels in which each jewel reflects every other (Flower Garland, as Huayan explains it)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vimalakirti answered by saying nothing at all, and later readers heard thunder. Your line: thunderous silence.

Dew hangs on a spider's web at sunrise. Lean in close to one drop and there's the whole garden inside it, tiny and curved. Lean closer and the next drop over is in there too, and inside that drop is this one. Two drops, each holding the other. Now let that run across the whole web. Remember Fazang's golden lion, and the lamp in a room of mirrors? Today, the huge sutra of visions behind them. Today's word is its name: Avatamsaka, the Flower Garland.
screen: `DEW ON A WEB.` → `EACH DROP HOLDS ANOTHER.` → `THE FLOWER GARLAND.`

segments.voice: The Avatamsaka Sutra, usually called the Flower Garland in English, isn't built like an argument. It's built like a vision. Buddhas fill worlds, light pours from them, and the scenes keep opening inside one another. In China a school grew up around it, called Huayan, which is the Chinese name of the sutra, and its teachers needed pictures for what the sutra was showing. One is Indra's net. As Huayan tells it, in the heaven of the god Indra hangs a net stretching out in every direction. At every knot there's a jewel, polished so clear that it reflects every other jewel in the net, and each of those reflections holds the reflections of all the others, without end. Look into one jewel and you're looking at the entire net. The point isn't only that everything is connected. A string of causes is connected too: the farmer, the rain, the truck, the cup of coffee. Huayan says more. Each thing actually holds the whole. One in all, all in one. And here's the detail that's easy to miss: the jewels don't melt into one big glow. Each stays a single jewel in its own place, and that's exactly why it can reflect the others. Tradition says a Huayan teacher once showed this to a ruler of China by setting mirrors all around a lamp, so the one flame appeared everywhere at once. The net shows up in small places too: one person's mood filling a whole room, a whole family visible in one child's face.
screen: `A SUTRA BUILT LIKE A VISION.` · `A NET OF JEWELS IN INDRA'S HEAVEN.` · `EACH JEWEL SHOWS THE WHOLE NET.` · `EACH JEWEL STAYS ITSELF.` · then, large: `EACH REFLECTS ALL.`

segments.voice: Find something that reflects: a window, a glass of water, a dark phone screen, the back of a spoon. Look at what's caught there, then look again more slowly, and notice the glass showing things it isn't while staying exactly itself. If a second surface is nearby, see whether one shows the other.
Avatamsaka. The Flower Garland Sutra, whose Huayan teachers pictured everything as a net of jewels, each one reflecting all the rest. Today's word.
Your line: each reflects all. The smallest drop on the web holds the whole garden. Day eleven ninety-three, done.

howItsDone: In the Huayan tradition of China, and in schools that grew from it in Korea and Japan, Indra's net is a classic teaching image for how all things contain and reflect one another.
